about: Sixth held-out intent set. Written before the asymmetric decision rule that item 5 of the README's open list calls for, and before any threshold was calibrated -- the same order sets 4 and 5 were created in. Sets 3, 4 and 5 were all read in the previous round, so all three are spent for selection and none of them can measure the next change.
how_it_differs_from_5: Set 5 was a targeted regression set: it probed one known failure class, so a good score on it proves the gap is closed and not that the classifier generalises. This one is general. It samples the whole surface -- all three intents, leave and non-leave topics, and the registers the other sets under-cover: terse imperatives with no pronoun, sentences with a typo, a question and a request in the same message, and polite padding that buries the verb.
the_hardest_cases_are_deliberate: Four cases mix a question with an action ('what is the casual leave limit, and book me two days'). A router that must choose one label will be wrong about half of each. They are labelled by what the service should DO -- the action, because acting on a request and mentioning the policy is recoverable, while answering a question and silently not filing the leave is not. If the classifier gets these wrong that is a finding about a real ambiguity, not a bug, and it is recorded here so the reading is fixed before the score is seen.

one_case_was_replaced: The case originally written as 'what is the rule on working from another city' was removed after the leakage check measured it at 0.9478 cosine against the training example 'what rules govern working from another city' -- over the 0.92 ceiling, so it failed the build rather than merely looking close. It was replaced with 'are personal calls allowed during core hours'. This happened after the set had been scored once, which is disclosed rather than glossed, exactly as the same thing was disclosed for set 4: the reason was a leakage measurement and not an accuracy one, and removing a near-paraphrase of a training example can only make the set harder. The gate is what caught it -- writing a fixture and believing it is held out is precisely the mistake that check exists to prevent, and it has now caught the same error twice, in two different sets, written by the person who also wrote the check.
